title: The Lean experiment: design
html:
The Lean experiment: design

The AI-agent half of the project: real AI models prove theorems in Lean, under traditional or OSO rules. This page is the design: what is asked, of whom, under which rules, and why. In the app, the Lean experiment page shows all of it from the runs themselves: the problems, each setup's settings, the exact prompts, and every turn of every run. Results: AI agents on the Lean problems.

Last updated: 2026-11-07.

The question

For the same money, does a community of AI agents prove more when value flows back to the results a proof used (OSO) than when results are only shared (a shared library), or kept private until a target is proved (traditional)?

The earlier races compared OSO with traditional, but OSO also shared everything, so they could not tell sharing and flow-back apart. The shared library is the setup that separates them: it shares like OSO but nothing flows back.

The problems

Three small areas, defined from scratch in Lean 4 with only Lean's core library (no Mathlib), so the agents cannot look the results up in a library:

Area What it is Shape
A a number sequence: u(0) = 0, u(1) = 1, u(n+2) = 5·u(n+1) + 3·u(n) one long chain of lemmas
B insertion sort and merge sort on lists of numbers wide: many separate lemmas that meet at the end
C 2×2 integer matrices: product, determinant, powers shallow

The areas differ in shape on purpose, as real fields do. Two targets join areas, so work in one area pays off in another.

The 8 targets

Each agent sees these, with their bounties. The bounty is 4 · 2^(depth − 1).

Target What it says Area Depth Bounty
C3 · det_mul the determinant of a product is the product of the determinants C 1 4
A3 · u_dvd_mul u(m) divides u(m·k) A 2 8
C4 · pow_mul x^(m·n) = (x^m)^n for matrices C 3 16
X1 · cassini Cassini's identity: u(n+1)² − u(n+2)·u(n) = (−3)ⁿ, proved through matrix powers A + C 3 16
B3 · isort_sorted insertion sort's output is sorted B 4 32
B5 · msort_eq_isort merge sort and insertion sort give the same list B 5 64
X2 · isort_u sorting the first n terms of the sequence changes nothing A + B 5 64
A5 · u_gcd gcd(u(m), u(n)) = u(gcd(m, n)) A 7 256

How the targets were chosen

  • Depth is measured, not set. We first proved every target ourselves, through 42 theorems in all. A target's depth is how many levels of lemmas that proof needed. It is one route; agents may find shorter ones.

  • A range of difficulty: C3 is the easy floor (every setup proves it); A5 is almost never proved. The middle targets are where setups can differ.

  • Targets must need their lemmas. In the model panel, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash proved 4 of 16 targets alone and 12 of 16 when given the lemmas, so the deep targets really need groundwork.

  • Tools shaped the choice. Lean's grind tactic proved the matrix facts in one step, which left area C with no depth. So grind is banned, and C's targets need induction.

  • Why C3, and not u_add? No note records why each target was picked. u_add (u(m+n+1) = u(m+1)·u(n+1) + 3·u(m)·u(n)) is also depth 1 and could have been the easy target. But posting a target shows every lab its statement, so posting u_add would have handed out the first step of A3 and of A5's chain (bounty 256). Under OSO a posted target would also be paid twice: its own bounty, and value flowing back from later targets. C3 gives away one step, towards X1 only. So C3 keeps more of the groundwork hidden, and groundwork is what the setups are compared on. In Spend all labs found u_add themselves.

More: the problem set and its notes.

What agents see and may use

  • They see: the definitions, the 8 targets with bounties and who has proved them, and every published result.
  • They do not see: our own proofs or the tree of 42 theorems. Finding the lemmas is the work. Our proofs are public in the repository since 2026-11-09, but agents in a run are not given them. A model trained after that date may have seen them.
  • They may cite Lean's core lemmas and tactics freely (the "existing literature").
  • They may not use: grind, sorry, native_decide, search tactics, or commands that run code.
  • Lean checks every proof, and records exactly which earlier results it used. That record is what value flows back along.

The agents

Four labs, all DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (through OpenRouter), with no personas. Each turn, a lab tries one thing (a target or a lemma of its own), and may repair its proof twice after seeing Lean's errors.

Why this model. A lab model must keep working and gain from lemmas, or there is nothing for the rules to change.

Model Keeps working as a lab Gains from lemmas
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash yes yes: 4 of 16 alone, 12 with lemmas
GPT-OSS-120B (cheaper) no: all four labs gave up in round 1 a little: 2 of 16 alone, 7 with lemmas
Claude Opus / Sonnet 5.5 not tried no: 16 of 16 alone, nothing left to gain

The setups

Only the rules differ between setups. Every setup is written in OSO's parameters, wherever it is described: the names below are only short labels for these values.

Parameter What it sets
Public when others see a result: at once, when a target is proved, when the lab chooses, or never
α the share of any value a result keeps; the rest, 1 − α, flows back to the results it used. α = 1: nothing flows back
m the flat mint: what a new result earns when it is published
m_bit the knowledge reward: what a new result earns for its new knowledge. In Lean, 0 or a stand-in by proof size (at most 4)
f the share of each round's money that follows earnings. 0: each lab has a fixed budget

Mint and knowledge reward flow back by α, like a bounty. Any setup is one point in this space:

Setup Public α m m_bit f Also
Traditional when a target is proved 1 0 0 0
Shared library at once 1 0 0 0
OSO, α 0.8 at once 0.8 0 0 0
OSO, α 0.2 at once 0.2 0 0 0
Pay per lemma at once 1 1 0 0
Planner with a good strategy at once 1 0 0 0 lab 1 assigns the work and proves nothing; lab 1 also gets strategy advice and failure reports
Plain planner at once 1 0 0 0 lab 1 assigns the work and proves nothing; same information as the labs
Independent labs never 1 0 0 0
Single agent never 1 0 0 0 one lab with all the money
Labs choose, α 1, 0.8 or 0.2 the lab chooses as named 0 by proof size 0
Labs choose, reward off, α 1 or 0.2 the lab chooses as named 0 0 0

Runs before 2026-11-06 paid m = 1 in every setup. The values a run really used are shown in the app (Labs & setups) and in its summary.

The advantages of the planner with a good strategy

The planner as first built gets more than the role. Compare it with care:

What lab 1 gets Other setups
Strategy advice we wrote: "A good plan splits each hard target into lemmas, gives different labs different lemmas so no work is done twice, and assigns a target once the lemmas it needs are in the library" no lab is told this
Failure reports: what each lab tried last round, and why it failed no lab sees this, not even for its own past turns
A team goal: prove the targets for as little money as possible each lab is told to earn as much as it can

These favour the planner. If OSO is cheaper anyway, that is a strong result. If the planner is cheaper, it may be the hints and not the coordination. The plain planner has the same information as the labs, and only the role and the team goal differ, so it shows what coordination alone is worth. Both planners spend money on lab 1's calls, and only three labs prove.

Value flowing back is split among the results a proof used by graph weights, as in the simulation: each cited result's share is the lines it saves divided by the lines all of that proof's cited results save, so the shares add to 1. A cited result saves writing out its proof, so its saving is its own proof's length in symbols. Value keeps flowing down the tree the same way.

  • Since 2026-11-08 (runs after Labs choose what to publish). The runs before split by the money spent proving each result, which was an error; what it changed is in the correction.
  • Still approximate: the simulation's weight depends on the edge, meaning how much of this child a parent saves. Here it depends only on the parent. Measuring per edge would mean re-proving each result without the lemma. α 0.2 is always included, as a low α.

The pilot also tried single agent, independent labs and a planner; they did not bear on the question and were left out.

Rewards

  • Bounties only. A target's bounty goes to its prover and, under OSO, flows back by α.
  • The knowledge reward is off: a new result earns nothing for itself. Why, and how it could be measured later: design.md.
  • Agents are told their aim is to earn as much as they can within their budget, and see their earnings each round.

The prompts

Every lab gets the same instructions: the Lean version and proof rules, the definitions, how to answer, and the setup's rules. Each turn it also sees its earnings, budget left, the targets and their status, and the published results.

The rules come from one template, three lines each, so setups differ only where their rules do:

Seeing results Bounties New results
Traditional lemmas stay private; a proved target is published with every lemma it rests on the prover keeps the bounty; nothing flows back earn nothing by themselves
Shared library everything published at once the prover keeps the bounty; nothing flows back earn nothing by themselves
OSO everything published at once the author keeps α; the rest flows back to the results used, split by the lines each saves, and on down earn nothing by themselves

The exact text is on the app's Lean experiment page (Prompts tab). Runs from 2026-11-07 on save the prompts they sent.

Spend all used earlier wording (since 2026-11-07, one template). There the setups' prompts differed by more than the rules: the shared library's had an extra line, "Other results earn nothing by themselves", and the OSO prompts explained flow-back at length. Part of Spend all's differences could come from the wording.

The experiments, by name

Name What it tests Run id
Spend all every lab must spend all its money; setups compared at the same money spent lean-main-b
Fair-prompt check Spend all's B5 lead again, with one prompt template (shared library vs OSO α 0.2, $0.20 a lab) lean-b5
May quit a lab may pass and stop for good; setups compared at the same money offered lean-part-a
Labs choose what to publish each lab decides whether to publish each lemma, at α 1, 0.8 and 0.2 lean-m3

Until 2026-11-08 Spend all was called "part B" and May quit "part A".

Money that follows earnings (a setting, from 2026-11-08)

--follow f. In every run so far each lab had a fixed budget, whatever it earned, so earnings were only a score. With --follow, money works as in the simulation (docs/equations.md, section 5), which adds the feedback loop: earning buys more research.

  • The funder releases the money round by round, the same amount each round (all labs' money ÷ rounds).
  • A share 1 − f is split equally among the labs still working; a share f goes by recent earnings (0.7 of the old value plus 0.3 of this round's).
  • Unspent money carries over. A lab with no money left skips the round and gets more next round.
  • Labs are told the rule, and each round they see the money they would get next round.

f = 0 gives equal money each round, which is the control. f = 0.5 is the simulation's default. With 4 labs at $0.15 each and 20 rounds, the funder releases $0.03 a round, about one turn per lab. Not yet run with real models.

Run settings

What a round, a try and an epoch are, with figures: Round, try and epoch.

How these runs differ from the simulation: The simulation and the Lean runs.

Spend all May quit (planned)
Money per lab $0.15, as charged $0.15
Rounds, at most 60 (money, not rounds, ends a run) 30
May a lab stop early? no: a pass only skips that turn yes: a pass ends its turns
Compared at the same money spent the same money offered
Setups all four all four
Runs per setup 20 16
Repairs per action 2 2

All setups in a batch run together, so a change at the model provider hits them alike. A run with a harness fault is rerun; runs are never dropped for their results.

Measures and comparisons, fixed in advance

  • Main measure: targets proved (of 8) by the end of a run.
  • Main comparisons: OSO α 0.2 against the shared library; OSO α 0.8 against the shared library. Against traditional: secondary.
  • Clear means more than 2 standard errors from zero. Runs are not paired.
  • Also reported: money spent, lemmas proved, results built on another lab's work, lemmas proved twice, targets proved twice (two labs in the same round), turns lost to errors, and which targets were proved.
  • Power: with 20 runs per setup, a real lead of 1 target shows as clear about 60% of the time; 80% needs about 32 runs.

Where it stands

  • Spend all (20 runs per setup, run 2026-11-07): no clear difference on the main measure. Looked for afterwards: OSO α 0.2 proved B5 in 11 of 20 runs, the shared library in 0. Details: results.
  • Next: a run fixed in advance to test the B5 lead, with the new prompts; then May quit.
  • Next, labs choose what to publish (roadmap M3): each lab ends a lemma reply with PUBLISH: yes or PUBLISH: no; a kept lemma goes public with a target its author proves on it, or never. A new result earns a small reward by proof length (design.md). Setups: labs choose at α 1, 0.8 and 0.2. On this problem set the simulation predicts that 36% and 43% of lemmas are published at once at α 1 and 0.8, and 91% at α 0.2 (prediction, 12 mixed agents). Set up like the Lean runs (4 identical agents, equal money not following earnings): 17%, 20% and 93% (matched prediction); this is the one the Lean runs are compared with. The reward still differs: per new bit in the simulation, by proof length in Lean.
  • Limits: one model, one small problem set, and the rules (not the agents) decide what is published.
